articles.title: "Best take I've ever seen": Jackson Chourio's walk-off hit for Brewers in postseason almost didn't happen
articles.standfirst: The Milwaukee Brewers took a 2-0 series lead over the San Diego Padres in dramatic fashion on Sunday.
articles.summary: The Milwaukee Brewers took a 2-0 series lead over the San Diego Padres in dramatic fashion on Sunday.
articles.body:
The odds were stacked against the Milwaukee Brewers on Sunday. The San Diego Padres went into the bottom of the 9th inning with a 3-2 lead and had the nearly unhittable Mason Miller on the mound. Yet the Brewers found a way.

It took until the final out - in fact, until the final strike. But Jackson Chourio finished the game with a walk-off, two-run single that sent American Family Field into a frenzy. The only reason it even happened was due to what MLB analyst Ben Verlander called possibly " the best take I've ever seen ".

Jackson Chourio somehow held off on Mason Miller's slider after 104 mph fastball with the count at 1-2

Chourio was ahead 1-0 in the count to start the at-bat, only to fall behind 1-2 after a swinging strike and a foul ball. The first three pitches were all high-velocity fastballs: 102 mph, 102 mph, and 104 mph . On the fourth pitch, Miller tried to ring up Chourio with a low slider , but Chourio refused to chase it . On the next pitch, Miller went back to the fastball, and Chourio hit a liner into center field to end the game.

The reason the take on 1-2 was so impressive was that Miller was setting it up with his fastballs . To a hitter, that slider Miller threw starts in the strike zone, only to quickly dip down completely out of it . Chourio appeared to be looking for it.

At 2-2, Chourio was in a much more favorable count. Miller could have gone with a breaking ball again, but he ran the risk of throwing a ball and bringing the count to a full 3-2 . With the bases loaded, that would have been precarious. In the end, Chourio won the at-bat, and the game.

articles.title: Who is Front Row Amy? The Brewers fan that went viral on social media
articles.standfirst: The 58-year-old Milwaukee supporter has attracted national attention simply by attending games and keeping score
articles.summary: The 58-year-old Milwaukee supporter has attracted national attention simply by attending games and keeping score
articles.body:
Every October, millions of baseball fans tune into the MLB playoffs and discover familiar faces sitting behind home plate. Few have become as recognizable as Amy Williams , the Milwaukee supporter affectionately known as Front Row Amy .

The 58-year-old has spent years watching the Milwaukee Brewers from one of the best seats at American Family Field, carefully recording every pitch while television cameras capture her distinctive outfits and enthusiastic reactions.

Yet Williams has never particularly sought the attention. She considers herself an ordinary baseball supporter whose passion for the Brewers unexpectedly turned her into an internet personality.

"I'm just a normal person. I'm just a normal fan like anyone else who really, really loves the Brewers," she told the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel.

Who is Front Row Amy and how did she become famous?

Williams lives in Oshkosh, Wisconsin, roughly 90 minutes from Milwaukee, where she works as an accountant for her family's property management business.

Her baseball obsession began relatively late, in 2007, when she watched the Brewers while recovering from surgery and became fascinated by the sport.

"It was really exciting and I just was hooked from that first game that I watched," Williams recalled.

She purchased season tickets the following year before moving into Section 117, Row 1, Seat 5 in 2011, establishing the routine that eventually made her famous.

Williams typically attends around 40 regular-season games annually, often traveling alone, and uses a specialized scorebook to document pitches, plays and memorable moments.

"It's a huge part of my life," she explained. "I can't imagine not just being a die-hard fan of the Brewers."

Her regular appearances eventually attracted attention from sports radio, national websites and social media, with a Front Row Amy bobblehead even produced in recognition of her popularity.

Why Front Row Amy stepped away from the spotlight

Although Williams initially enjoyed becoming a recognizable figure, the experience changed when online criticism began overshadowing the positive interactions.

"It's not all it's cracked up to be," she admitted, explaining that she eventually closed her Facebook page and website.

She still has more than 31,000 followers on X, although she now prefers maintaining a lower profile and concentrating on the baseball itself.

That passion produced another unforgettable moment on October 4, when Jackson Chourio delivered a walk-off single against the San Diego Padres on Williams' 58th birthday.

"That was amazing. I kind of forgot it was my birthday because I was so focused on the game," she said.

Will Front Row Amy have to change famous nickname?

Williams faces an unexpected adjustment next season because renovations to American Family Field's premium seating will introduce another row directly in front of her usual position.

Although she will retain her existing seat, the change effectively makes it a second-row location, raising the possibility that Front Row Amy could become Second Row Amy.

The adjustment also comes with a substantial ticket-price increase, although Williams remains primarily concerned about maintaining an unobstructed view of the pitchers.

She has witnessed countless memorable Brewers moments, including postseason victories and historic individual performances, and has no intention of abandoning that tradition.

Asked how much longer she plans to keep attending games, Williams offered a characteristically simple response: "As long as I can."
